name: AMD MI300X: measured power-limit sweep finds efficiency peak hardware- and workload-specific, and power limits below 400 W are not respected
unit: W - the power-limit floor below which the MI300X did not honour the requested cap in this study
methodology: Measured, not modelled: the RRZE-HPC framework runs vision (image classification and generation) and LLM (continued pre-training and inference) benchmarks on NVIDIA H100, NVIDIA H200 and AMD MI300X while sweeping the enforced power cap. Energy efficiency is defined by the authors as throughput / (P_GPU + 100 W / N_GPU), with a constant 100 W per node added as an estimated fixed system overhead beyond the accelerators - so their efficiency numbers are NOT pure-GPU figures and cannot be compared to a bare-GPU joules/token. Metric 'quality' is a placeholder because the enum has no energy metric; the number is a power cap in watts. Code and data are public (github.com/RRZE-HPC/hpc-ai-perf-bench, Zenodo 20083679), so this is the reproducible entry in this group.
notes: TWO RESULTS WORTH KEEPING, BOTH NON-NVIDIA. (1) POWER-CAP FLOOR: 'amd-smi did not allow power state modifications, and the MI300X did not respect power limits set below 400 W' - so a power-capped MI300X energy measurement below 400 W is not measuring what the cap says it is. This is the AMD-side twin of the MLPerf MaxQ gotcha already in the repo (mlperf-maxq-is-not-a-watt-cap): a vendor power-control surface that looks authoritative and is not. (2) MI300X SHAPE: the MI300X had the LOWEST overall energy efficiency of the three accelerators but the FLATTEST response to rising power limits, and the authors tie that flatness to a power-limit-dependent change in MEMORY CLOCK on the AMD platform - i.e. on AMD the cap is partly enforced by dropping memory clock, not just core clock, so a cap-induced slowdown is not a clean core-clock experiment. By contrast H100 efficiency peaks at 300-400 W depending on workload and H200 at ~400 W with flatter high-power behaviour. NO JOUles/TOKEN FIGURE FOR MI300X IS RECORDED: this paper reports work units per Joule, not tokens per joule, and converting would require assuming a throughput the paper does not tabulate per token.
